description: Vamos criar uma Jukebox da Terra!
summary: Earth Jukebox lets anyone hear how the temperature of their own city has changed since 1950. It is a mobile-first web app that you can hear and see, designed with blind and low-vision users in mind and open to everyone. It turns NASA's global temperature anomaly map (SVS 5207, GISTEMP v4) into music. You pick a city. For every year from 1950 to 2023, the app reads the color of the map's pixel over that city, converts it to a value using the map's own legend (−2 to +2 °C), and uses that value to choose and mix the sounds of the year. One bar equals one year, so the whole story plays in about 2 minutes 40 seconds. A piano melody shows whether the temperature is heading up or down, and a background tone climbs as the city gets warmer. Carbon dioxide (NOAA) and local rainfall (NASA POWER) add context. Screen-reader announcements, keyboard control and a tape-rewind effect for time travel make the experience accessible. The sound you hear is the color NASA's map has over your city.
details:
What it does. Earth Jukebox pairs a frame from NASA's Earth Information Center content (the SVS 5207 global temperature anomaly visualization) with a soundtrack built from that frame's colors. The listener chooses a city by GPS or by typing its name, and hears 1950 to 2023, one bar per year, while the map, a lens over the city, the value and a chart follow the music.

What you are hearing. The temperature anomaly: how much warmer or cooler a year was than the 1951–1980 average of the same place. In climate science "anomaly" simply means a difference from a reference, which lets very different cities be compared. A piano figure in each bar shows where the temperature goes next year (flat, small, medium or large rise or fall). A second layer changes when the value crosses −1, 0 and +1 °C on the map's own scale, so two cities can be compared by ear. Peaks, valleys and record-hot years have short accents.

How it works.

  1. The app ships one image per year of the SVS 5207 visualization (frames downloaded from NASA's SVS site and resized to 1280×720 WebP).
  2. In the browser, it converts the city's latitude and longitude to a pixel of the Robinson-projected map, takes the median color of a 5×5 pixel window and matches it to the color legend printed inside the frame. The result is the anomaly in °C for each year.
  3. A track is built for that city: which bar plays each year, which layers sound, and which events (records, droughts) get a card and an accent.
  4. Layers are recorded loops (the rain sounds are synthesized by a script) and bars locked to a fixed tempo (110 BPM, D minor). The code chooses and mixes them live, with Tone.js, from the values read off the frames. It never retunes or time-stretches them. The sound is therefore assembled in real time in the browser from the frame colors, but it is not synthesized from scratch.
  5. Context layers: carbon dioxide from the NOAA Mauna Loa record (1959–2023) adds voices as the concentration grows, and local rainfall from NASA POWER (from 1981) plays a kalimba that gets busier with more rain.

The sounds, in short. Everything is in D minor at 110 BPM, so any combination sounds like one piece.

  • Temperature melody (piano): seven one-bar figures. Flat, small, medium or large rise, and small, medium or large fall. Every figure starts and ends near D, so any bar can follow any other.
  • Temperature level (piano): four loops, one for each band of the map's scale (below −1 °C, −1 to 0, 0 to +1, above +1 °C). The pitch gets higher as the band gets warmer.
  • Carbon dioxide (low organ and strings): five voices that stack up as the NOAA concentration grows. A single low D closes the piece in 2023.
  • Rainfall (kalimba): four loops, from two notes to five. Rain rising a lot plays more notes; rain dropping a lot plays fewer. Extreme rain and drought have a short accent each.

Accessibility. Designed with blind and low-vision people in mind, and useful to everyone: screen-reader labels and a live region that announces the city, the year, events and the end of the piece; full keyboard control; large touch targets; high-contrast retrofuturist design aiming at WCAG AA; reduced-motion support. Time travel works like rewinding a tape, with the music itself playing backwards and a tick per year. The page opens in English and °F, with Portuguese and °C one tap away (the app shows both units side by side).

Benefits and intended impact. A global map is hard to read even for sighted people, and out of reach for blind users. This turns "the planet is warming" into something personal and audible: you hear your city, year after year. It can be used in classrooms, museums and by anyone who prefers listening to looking.

Creativity. The music was composed so that any bar can follow any other. Every loop is one bar at 110 BPM in D minor, and the seven melodic figures all start and end near D, so the code can choose a different bar for each year and the result still sounds like one piece. The code only adjusts volume, never pitch or tempo. The rules follow the data and the map's own legend: four loops for the four bands of the scale (below −1 °C, −1 to 0, 0 to +1, above +1 °C), five carbon dioxide voices that stack up as concentration grows and end on a single low D, and a kalimba whose notes grow from two to five with rainfall. The piano and CO₂ loops were composed and recorded by a doctor of music on our team; AI assistance was used only to splice the loops. The rain sounds were designed by a team member and synthesized by a script. Every city gets a different track because every city has a different color history.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Tone.js (audio); d3 and d3-geo-projection (map projection and chart); Open-Meteo Geocoding and BigDataCloud (city search and reverse geocoding); GitHub Pages (hosting); Python and Node scripts to prepare the frames and to synthesize the rain sounds.

Use of AI. The website code was developed with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), directed by our team, who defined the concept, the musical mapping and the design decisions. The rain sounds were synthesized by a script written with AI assistance, the music loops were spliced with AI help, a small fallback list of cities (used only if the city search fails) was created with AI assistance, and parts of the documentation were written with AI assistance.

Honest limits. One visualization (temperature) is read from NASA frames; CO₂ and rainfall come from data series and give context. Values read from colors are accurate to about ±0.1 °C. The map is a 24-month moving average, so each year is a smoothed value. If NASA POWER cannot be reached, the rainfall layer is switched off and the app says so. The rain sounds are synthesized by a script, not recorded. The audio has not yet been tested with blind and low-vision listeners.

Acknowledgement. The rainfall data was obtained from National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Langley Research Center's Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) project funded through the NASA Earth Science Division (accessed 2026/11/15). City search uses Open-Meteo, with GeoNames data.

Source code. https://github.com/zecazeco/NASAspaceappschallenge (MIT license; audio under CC0).
